1st edition (1859) - breeding assumption: brings forth three pair (6 young) in the interval between 30 and 90 years old; survival age not specified.  
6th edition (1872) - breeding assumption: brings forth six young in the interval between 30 and 90 years old; survives till 100 years old.  

1st edition (1859) - time period: at the end of the fifth century (500 years).  
6th edition (1872) - time period: after a period of from 740 to 750 years.  

1st edition (1859) - result: fifteen million elephants.  
6th edition (1872) - result: nearly nineteen million elephants.  

The first edition assumed the elephant produces three pairs (6 young) and after 500 years there would be 15 million elephants; the sixth edition changed to producing six young, living to 100 years, and after 740–750 years there would be nearly 19 million elephants.

Population increases in a geometrical ratio, subsistence only in an arithmetical ratio; and Malthus takes as his rule that unchecked population doubles itself every twenty-five years.

Mill - On Liberty: Enslaving the soul itself through social tyranny and the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling.

Tocqueville - Democracy in America: Checking the development of leading characters and being felt more in the manners than in the conduct of society.

Both identify a form of social or moral oppression beyond legal and official power, but Mill emphasizes the deep penetration into individual life and soul, while Tocqueville highlights the stifling of exceptional character and the influence on national manners.

Mill - On Liberty: Majority feeling in the United States operates as a tolerably effectual sumptuary law, and in many parts of the Union it is really difficult for a person possessing a very large income, to find any mode of spending it, which will not incur popular disapprobation.

Veblen - The Theory of the Leisure Class: The accepted standard of expenditure in the community or class largely determines what his standard of living will be, through popular insistence on conformity to the accepted scale of expenditure as a matter of propriety, under pain of disesteem and ostracism.

Mill describes majority feeling as a social constraint that directly makes showy spending difficult; Veblen explains that this feeling restrains the motive to deviate from the accepted standard of expenditure, because non-conformity invites disesteem and ostracism.
